title: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: despite the simplicity of their rules, the behavior of the programs was often far from simple. Indeed, even some of the very simplest programs that I looked at had behavior that was as complex as anything I had ever seen.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “An Outline of Basic Ideas” (from p. 1), p. 2. Scope: simple programs such as elementary cellular automata, enumerated systematically

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Systematic enumerations are public and easy to reproduce. They can strongly test the claim in specified program families, but the words often, simplest, and as complex as any known prevent a fully scope-matched decision.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate explicitly bounded families of short programs, run them from standardized initial conditions, and measure compressibility, entropy, and structural diversity. Compare the observed frequency and maxima with prespecified thresholds for simple versus complex behavior.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No finite enumeration establishes the claim across all simple programming formalisms.

Complexity and simplicity admit multiple inequivalent measures.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.62
discriminating power: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The scope is the systematic enumeration of simple programs, which is a finite computation for the usual small rule spaces. Open simulators regenerate every elementary pattern in seconds, and a pre-registered classifier turns 'often far from simple' into a count. The superlative comparison with 'any known' complexity is the soft edge, and it does not block a yes-or-no test of the main quantitative reading.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate elementary cellular automata and other small rule spaces from simple seeds, and classify each space-time pattern as periodic, nested, or incompressible under a fixed compression and periodicity test. The claim is confirmed if a substantial fraction is not periodic or nested, and refuted if complex patterns are absent or confined to rules that are not simple.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Compression and statistical tests can miss hidden regularity.

How often is 'often,' and 'as complex as any known' depends on the complexity measure.
